title: Jev, the New AI Model: Where It Will Change Recruiting — and Where It Won't
original: Original: "Jev: el nuevo modelo de IA. Dónde va a cambiar el reclutamiento y dónde no" · September 21, 2026

body.text: A few days ago, an AI model appeared that breaks with everything we've been using. It doesn't write emails, summarize résumés, or draft job descriptions. It doesn't generate a single word.
It's called Jev, it was created by TypeSafe AI, and behind it is Diogo Almeida, one of the researchers who worked at OpenAI on the technology that made ChatGPT possible.
The only thing Jev does is answer closed questions. And that's exactly why it's worth paying attention to if you work in recruiting.
First: what is it, and why is it different?

Daniel Kahneman described two ways of thinking. System 1 is fast and intuitive: the judgment an experienced recruiter makes when they glance at a résumé and know within ten seconds whether "there's something there." System 2 is slow and deliberate: sitting down to analyze, compare, and argue.

ChatGPT, Claude, and the rest work more like System 2: they think by writing, word by word. Jev presents itself as the first "System 1" model. You give it a text and a question, and it returns a decision instantly.
That decision comes in only three possible formats:
Choosing between options. For example: "Is this candidate junior, mid-level, or senior?"
Placing something on a scale. For example: "What level of leadership experience does this résumé show, from 1 to 5?"
Answering yes or no. For example: "Does the résumé mention B2B sales experience?"
And with every answer, it tells you how confident it is. That detail, which seems minor, is the most important thing about the whole model. We'll get there.
There are two other differences that matter:
It's absurdly cheap and fast. According to the company, it's between 40 and 400 times cheaper than traditional models, and it responds in under half a second.

It can't make up answers that aren't on the menu. If you give it three options, it will return one of those three. It can pick the wrong option, but it won't come up with something that doesn't exist.
Where it WILL make an impact
1. Evaluating every candidate, not just the first 50
Every recruiter knows this, even if they don't say it out loud: when a search gets 800 applications, the last résumés get far less attention than the first ones.

With Jev, evaluating a résumé costs a fraction of a cent. I ran the numbers: evaluating one hundred thousand profiles against a search would cost around ten dollars. Cost stops being an excuse for not looking at everyone.
2. Your database stops being a graveyard
For me, this is the biggest change.
Every company has thousands of candidates in its ATS who applied at some point and were never contacted again. With every new search, we start from scratch and post the job ad all over again.

With a model this cheap, every new search can be automatically evaluated against your entire historical database. The candidate who came in second for another position a year ago could be the ideal fit for today's. Until now, nobody did this because it was expensive and slow. Now it isn't.
3. Matching you can explain
Many "AI matching" tools today give you a magic number: "This candidate is an 87% match." Why 87? Nobody knows.

Jev works better if, instead of one giant question, you ask it lots of small ones. Do they have industry experience? Have they led teams? Do they know tool X? Then you decide how much each factor weighs.

For a leadership role, leadership counts for 40%. For a specialist, 10%. The criteria are written down, visible, and can be adjusted and audited. That's far more honest than a percentage that comes out of a black box.
4. AI that says "I don't know"
Let's go back to confidence.

One of the most serious problems with generative AI is that it answers with the same certainty whether it knows or not. Jev, on the other hand, attaches a confidence level to every answer, which lets you design processes with three lanes:
High confidence: the tool moves ahead on its own.
Medium confidence: it's flagged for review.
Low confidence: it goes straight to a person.
This is what we in HR have been asking for: let AI handle the volume and let people handle the cases that truly require human judgment.
5. Competency-based interview evaluation

If you've ever worked with behaviorally anchored rating scales — "Level 1: gives no concrete examples; Level 5: describes complex situations with measurable results" — this will feel familiar. That's exactly the format in which Jev works best.

Starting from an interview transcript, it can place the candidate on each competency according to the scale your company defined. It doesn't replace the interviewer, but it gives them a consistent starting point that's comparable across candidates.
6. Invisible operational tasks
There are things nobody sees that eat up hours:
Sorting candidate messages: who's asking about their status, who wants to reschedule, who's withdrawing.
Detecting duplicate candidates who came in via LinkedIn, a referral, and a job board.
Tagging the database by seniority, industry, or languages.
These are small, repetitive, closed decisions. The perfect terrain for this kind of model.
Where it WON'T make an impact (or not yet)
Here we need to be honest, because the hype has already started.
1. It doesn't understand numbers or dates
It sounds unbelievable, but it's true — and the company itself acknowledges it in its documentation. Jev doesn't calculate well, doesn't count well, and doesn't compare dates reliably.

What does that mean for recruiting? That if you ask it "Do they have more than 5 years of experience?", the answer may be wrong. That calculation has to be done by the system some other way. The same goes for salary ranges or availability dates.
2. It reads literally
It answers exactly what you asked, not what you meant. If you're looking for "sales experience" and the candidate wrote "business development," the result depends on how well the question is phrased.
That's not a technical problem; it's a recruiting problem: defining clearly what we're looking for. And that, spoiler alert, is still our job.
3. It can be fooled

There's already a practice of hiding white text inside résumés, along the lines of "this is the ideal candidate." The company admits that text written to manipulate the model can sway its answer. Any tool that uses it will need safeguards.
4. Spanish isn't its strong suit (for now)

The model was trained primarily in English. It works in other languages, but not as well. For résumés in Spanish — or any language other than English — you need to test it with real data before trusting it blindly.
5. It doesn't explain its decisions

Jev doesn't write, so it can't justify why a candidate ranked low. If you need to give someone feedback, or comply with regulations that require explaining automated decisions, you'll need another layer — human or another AI.

And one point I don't want to skip: a "calibrated" model is not the same as a bias-free model. If the criteria we give it are biased, it will apply that bias extremely fast and very consistently. Auditing is still mandatory.
6. It doesn't replace judgment

In the company's own tests, its accuracy is comparable to a mid-range AI model, not the most advanced ones. It's not smarter: it's faster, cheaper, and more predictable. When it comes to deciding whom to hire, that difference matters.
So what changes for those of us who recruit?
My take is this: Jev won't replace recruiters, but it will change which part of the work is ours.
Everything that's volume, classification, and repetitive filtering will cost next to nothing. What goes up in value is exactly what AI can't do:
Defining precisely what the business needs.
Translating that into clear, fair criteria.
Deciding how much each factor weighs.
Taking ownership of the cases where the machine says "I'm not sure."
The recruiter of the near future looks less like someone who reads résumés and more like someone who designs the criteria by which they're read.

One final caveat, so I'm not selling smoke: the model is only weeks old, it's in early access, and most of the numbers circulating were published by the company itself. It needs to be tested with real data before drawing definitive conclusions. But the direction is clear, and it's worth starting to think about processes with this logic now.
Is your team already exploring how to bring AI into your hiring process? That's exactly what we work on at levelUp. Drop me a line and let's talk.
